title: Design of the tundra rainfall experiment (TRainEx) to simulate future summer precipitation scenarios
author: Grysko, Plekhanova, et al.
materials: Our field site, the Kytalyk research station, is located in the Kytalyk National Park in the Indigirka lowlands, northeast Siberia (70.83° N, 147.49° E; Fig. 1a). The region belongs to the continuous permafrost zone with an average active layer thickness of 42 cm. The 1981–2010 mean annual temperature of Chokurdakh, a village 28 km southeast of the Kytalyk research station, was -13.4 °C, with a mean July temperature of 10.3 °C. The 1981–2010 Chokurdakh mean annual precipitation was 196 mm, 39% of which fell between June and August [24]. The research area consists of two different morphological units: a drained thaw lake basin surrounded by remnants of Pleistocene yedoma deposits, floodplains, a few thermokarst lakes and drained thermokarst lakes (lakebed); and higher (10–30 m) plateaus with well-drained soils underlain with ice-rich permafrost (ridge). On both locations, the soil consists of silt overlain with 15–30 cm of peat. Morphological features include low and high centered ice wedge polygons and low palsas [25]. Vegetation at the Kytalyk research station primarily consists of dwarf shrub, moss tundra, and tussock sedge (Fig. 1b, c) based on the circumpolar Arctic vegetation map classification [26].Fig. 1Field site location and vegetation types. (a) Location of Kytalyk National Park, (b) ridge vegetation: tussock-sedge-dominated tundra, (c) drained lakebed vegetation: dwarf-shrub and moss-dominated tundra.Fig 1

steps.title: Record site coordinates and conditions
steps.instruction: Note the field site location at 70.83° N, 147.49° E in Kytalyk National Park, Indigirka lowlands, NE Siberia. Record average active layer thickness (42 cm), mean annual temperature (‑13.4 °C), mean July temperature (10.3 °C), mean annual precipitation (196 mm) and the proportion falling June‑August (39 %).

steps.title: Lay out experimental plot grid
steps.instruction: Establish 30 vegetation plots of 2 × 2 m each, arranged in 10 blocks (5 blocks per site). Place five blocks on the elevated ridge (tussock‑sedge tundra) and five on the drained lakebed (dwarf‑shrub tundra). Within each block, locate the three treatment plots (drought, extreme precipitation, control) with ~2 m spacing. Verify that vegetation height averages 12 ± 4 cm and that soil is silt overlain by 15–30 cm peat.

steps.title: Build shelter frames and install shingles
steps.instruction: Construct each 2.5 × 2.5 m shelter frame from 10 × 10 cm wooden beams, reinforced with steel L‑brackets, and add 5 × 5 cm support arms for the shingles. Attach ten transparent V‑profile acrylic glass shingles (model ‘GS 2458’, Bröking‑Plastex GmbH & Co. KG) per shelter; each shingle is 3 mm thick, 2.5 m long, with 101 mm flanges and a hypotenuse of 142.8 mm (shingle width). Orient shingles upward (channel‑facing) on drought shelters and downward on extreme‑precipitation and control shelters. Secure shingles with flexible metal bands (or heavy‑duty zip ties, not recommended for long‑term cold exposure). Ensure shelters face the prevailing wind direction to minimise wind disturbance.

substeps.instruction: Calculate required shingle number using InterceptedPrecipitation(%) = N × Width_shingle / Shelter_width × 100; with desired interception 57 %, shingle width 142.8 mm and shelter width 2500 mm, N = 10.
Leave a 25 cm margin around each plot (shelter size 2.5 × 2.5 m) to avoid edge effects.

steps.title: Install water collection and pump system
steps.instruction: Fit each drought shelter with a gutter that channels intercepted rain into a 208 L water‑retention tank. Place an AS88 SPXFlow automatic float switch inside the tank to trigger a 12 V Pacific Hydrostar marine utility pump (powered by a 12 V 7 Ah battery). Connect the pump to a 19 mm‑diameter, 8.5 m hose that runs to the paired extreme‑precipitation plot. Install two Rain Bird 8‑VAN sprinklers (5 cm nozzle diameter) at opposite corners of the irrigation plot. Insert a Gardena Smart flow meter in the hose between pump and sprinklers, and add a back‑flow valve before the flow meter. Regulate battery charging with a Campbell Scientific SP30 30 W solar panel and an ECO10 Phocos Eco charge controller. The system should activate roughly four times per average summer rain day (any day with liquid precipitation) to minimise standing water.

substeps.instruction: Connect the float switch to the pump so that water is pumped when tank level reaches the preset threshold.
Route the hose through the back‑flow valve to the flow meter, then to the two sprinklers.
Mount the pump, battery, solar panel and charge controller on the shelter frame, keeping all electrical components weather‑proof.

steps.title: Set up sensor network and data loggers
steps.instruction: Install HOBO data loggers (USB Micro Station HS 21) at each site. For each of the 30 plots, place a 0.5 × 0.5 m central sensor area containing two soil‑moisture sensors (HOBO S‑SMC‑M00, measurement range 0‑1 m³ m⁻³, uncertainty 0.031 m³ m⁻³) at 1 cm and 10 cm depth, and one soil‑temperature sensor (HOBO S‑TMB‑M00, ±0.2 °C) at 1 cm depth. Set sensor recording interval to 10 min. At each site, erect a weather station with a rain gauge (HOBO S‑RGF‑M00, ±0.2 mm) and two air‑temperature/relative‑humidity sensors (HOBO S‑THB‑M00, ±0.21 °C / ±2.5 %) positioned at 15 cm and 60 cm above ground. Record weather‑station data every 10 min during the growing season and every 30 min in the off‑season. Uninstall the rain gauge at the end of the growing season.

steps.title: Program pump activation schedule
steps.instruction: Configure the float‑switch‑controlled pump to run up to four times per rain day, based on the average number of rain events derived from the 73‑year summer precipitation record (mean 27.2 mm month⁻¹). Ensure the system pauses between runs to avoid algae growth and excess heat transfer to the soil.

steps.title: Perform winterization and storage
steps.instruction: At the end of the growing season, detach all shingles using the flexible metal bands (or zip ties) and store them in wooden shipping boxes placed away from the plots to prevent snow accumulation. Disconnect, drain, and remove all electrical components (pump, battery, solar panel, charge controller, flow meter, hoses, sprinklers) from the shelter frames and store them indoors. Leave the wooden frame structure in the field, as it is heavy enough to remain stable without anchoring into permafrost.

steps.title: Validate water delivery amounts
steps.instruction: During the summer, record water volume delivered by the flow meters and compare to rain‑gauge measurements. In 2019, the ten flow meters recorded an average of 89.4 L ± 6.4 L over two months, equivalent to 14.3 ± 1 mm of added precipitation (area 2.5 × 2.5 m). The rain gauge measured 21.6 ± 0.5 mm, of which 57 % (12.3 ± 0.3 mm) corresponds to the intended extreme‑precipitation addition. In 2020, one‑month flow‑meter data gave 55.2 L ± 5 L (8.8 ± 1 mm), while the Chokurdakh weather station reported 14.2 mm of ambient rain (57 % = 8.1 mm). Confirm that delivered water matches the target 57 % of ambient precipitation within experimental error.
